description: The hotspot game's words: one scene picture in the dark, searched with a flashlight whose battery is the clock. HAZARDS are what the learner must notice: each one is a reported decision, found (pressed) or missed (still unfound when the round ends); its id is a data-question-id row on the page, and its outcome codes are that row's data-measures, never in here. DECOYS are ordinary things in the same scene: pressing one costs a heart, and they are never reported. THE PICTURE DECIDES, NEVER THE WORDS: a label names the thing only, never its state, and each hazard should have a SAFE TWIN among the decoys -- the same thing done right, elsewhere in the picture, which may wear the same label -- so the learner must look to tell them apart. A spot's place is a fraction of the scene picture: x from its LEFT edge (a picture is not mirrored for Arabic), y from its top, r its radius as a fraction of the picture's width; keep spots apart, so one press never lands on two, and each circle inside the picture (y plus r times its width over its height at most 1), so no part of a spot is cut off. Ask the person for every rule and source you were not given.

title.description: The game's title, on its first screen and its debrief.

brief.description: The place, in one or two sentences, on the first screen; it is also what a screen reader says the scene picture shows. Never name a hazard here.

hazards.description: What the learner must notice, each over the thing in the picture it names. The condition that makes it a hazard (a handle past the edge, a medicine left open) is for the picture to show and the rule to say, never the label.

id.description: The interaction id the LMS receives: ASCII, unique in the lecture, and the data-question-id of one row on the page. Take it from the client's alignment document; never invent it.

label.description: What the light shows beside the spot: one to four words naming the thing only («علبة دواء»), never its state («مفتوحة») and never a verdict («خطر», «آمن»), so only the picture gives the answer. Its safe twin among the decoys may wear the same words.

x.description: The spot's centre across the picture, from its left edge: 0 is the left edge, 1 the right.

y.description: The spot's centre down the picture: 0 is the top, 1 the bottom.

r.description: The spot's radius as a fraction of the picture's width: 0.04 is a hand-sized thing in a room. At least 0.02, so a finger can press it.

rule.description: What makes it a hazard and what to do about it, in one sentence: shown when the learner finds it, and in the debrief.

source.description: The citation the learner reads under the rule («المصدر: …»). Ask the person; never invent it. Left empty, the release lists it as left for the person.

decoys.description: Ordinary things in the same scene, each over the thing it names -- best of all a safe twin of each hazard. Pressing one costs a heart; they are never reported, so they need no row on the page.

id.description: An ASCII name for the spot, unique among the hazards and the decoys; it is never reported.

label.description: What the light shows beside it, written like a hazard's label: the thing only, never its state.

x.description: Across the picture, from its left edge, as a hazard's x.

y.description: Down the picture, as a hazard's y.

r.description: Its radius as a fraction of the picture's width, as a hazard's r.

why.description: Optional: what makes it safe, in one sentence, shown when it is pressed and on the review sheet. Write it for a safe twin, so a learner who pressed it learns the difference.

slots.description: Optional: the art hand's own scene picture for the game's one picture slot (game.json names its size). The value is a path under the lecture's assets, such as "../assets/kitchen.png"; left out, the game shows its own placeholder scene, which the sample's spots fit. A new picture needs new spots.

scene.description: The place, seen whole, 16:9, opaque: every hazard and decoy visible in it at its x and y.
